Y7-029-A.label: Year 7 · Collecting like terms
Y7-029-A.title: Can we combine like terms?
Y7-029-A.why: Three x plus two x equals five x for every x. Both simplify to five x.
Y7-029-A.mis: Like terms have the same variable. Add their coefficients, not the letters.
bob: Look at the x terms on both sides.
We can replace x with a number to compare them.
Place the first value in the table. Multiply, then add.
Try a different value. Do both expressions still agree?
Two matching results are evidence, but not a general proof.
Collect the like terms: both forms are five x for every value.

Y7-029-B.label: Year 7 · A misleading match
Y7-029-B.title: Does one match prove a rule?
Y7-029-B.why: At x = 1, both give seven, but at x = 0 they give three and zero. One match cannot prove equivalence.
Y7-029-B.mis: Four x plus three is not seven x because three is a constant, not an x term.
bob: One expression has an x term and a fixed three.
Choose x equals one. Notice both sides give seven.
A single matching result does not prove a rule.
Test x equals zero and compare the outputs.
One difference is enough to disprove equivalence.
The constant three cannot be combined with four x.

Y9-006-A.label: Year 9 · Expanding a bracket
Y9-006-A.title: Are these two forms identical?
Y9-006-A.why: Distributivity gives 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 for all x, not just the values we tested.
Y9-006-A.mis: Multiply every term in the bracket. Doubling x alone is insufficient.
bob: Here are two algebraic expressions.
Test a value and find the result on each side.
Make another test to look for a difference.
Now expand the bracket, multiplying each term by two.
Both expressions simplify to two x plus six.
The distributive law proves they are equivalent.

Y9-006-B.label: Year 9 · Double brackets
Y9-006-B.title: Check the complete expansion
Y9-006-B.why: The four products are x², 3x, 2x and 6; combining them gives x² + 5x + 6.
Y9-006-B.mis: There are four products when two binomials multiply. Do not miss the constant product.
bob: Look carefully at the product of two brackets.
Substitute one number into the left and the right.
Try other values, including a negative one.
Now multiply every term in the first bracket by every term in the second.
Collect three x and two x into five x.
The complete expansion proves the identity.

Y9-006-C.label: Year 9 · Counterexample
Y9-006-C.title: Two matches can still mislead
Y9-006-C.why: At x = 0 and x = 1 the expressions match, but at x = 2 the values are four and two. They are not equivalent.
Y9-006-C.mis: Squaring a value is not the same as leaving it unchanged. Zero and one are special cases.
bob: The two expressions may appear to agree.
At zero, x squared and x both give zero.
At one, both expressions give one.
Look for a value that separates the results.
At two, four is not equal to two: that is a counterexample.
Equivalent expressions must agree for every permitted value.
